replacement: SOCRATES: At Naucratis, a city in Egypt, there lived a famous old god named Theuth. The bird called the Ibis is sacred to him, and he invented many arts: arithmetic, calculation, geometry, astronomy, checkers and dice. But his greatest discovery was the use of letters. In those days the god Thamus was king of all Egypt. He lived in the great city of Upper Egypt that the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god himself Ammon. Theuth came to him and showed him his inventions, asking that the rest of the Egyptians be allowed to have the benefit of them. He listed them one by one, and Thamus asked what each was used for. He praised some and found fault with others, as he approved or disapproved of them. It would take a long time to repeat everything Thamus said to Theuth in praise or blame of the various arts. But when they came to letters, Theuth said: 'This will make the Egyptians wiser and give them better memories. It is a specific both for the memory and for the wit.' Thamus replied: 'O most ingenious Theuth, the one who invents an art is not always the best judge of whether it will be useful or useless to those who use it. In this case, you are the father of letters, and out of fatherly love for your own children you have given them a quality they cannot have. This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, because they will stop using their memories. They will trust the external written characters and will not remember for themselves. The specific you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence. And you give your students not truth, but only the semblance of truth. They will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing. They will appear to know everything and will generally know nothing. They will be tiresome company, since they will have the show of wisdom without the reality.'

SOCRATES: No, it's not likely. In the garden of letters he will sow and plant, but only for recreation and amusement. He will write things down as memorials, to be treasured against the forgetfulness of old age, for himself or for any other old man walking the same path. He will enjoy watching their tender growth. And while others refresh their souls with banquets and the like, this will be the pastime in which he spends his days.
SOCRATES: Secondly, there is the criticism that was made of speaking or writing speeches, and how they might be rightly or wrongly criticized. Did our earlier argument not show —?

SOCRATES: That whether it is Lysias or any other writer who ever was or will be, private man or statesman, who proposes laws and so becomes the author of a political treatise and imagines that his work has great certainty and clearness, the mere fact that he writes in this way is a disgrace to him, whatever people may say. For not to know the nature of justice and injustice, and of good and evil, and not to be able to tell the dream from the reality, cannot in truth be anything but disgraceful to him, even if the whole world applauds him.
PHAEDRUS: Ask the same for me — friends should have all things in common.
